title: The World of Limitless Possibilities (with poem: Nine Gold Medals)

topics.title: Sports and inclusion: words that open doors

learn.hook: What makes a game truly great: the fastest player, or the moment when everyone gets to play?
points: The lesson 'The World of Limitless Possibilities' is linked with sport and inclusion: people of all abilities taking part.

Key words: inclusion (making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part), accessible (easy for everyone, including people with disabilities, to reach and use), empathy (understanding and sharing another person's feelings), perseverance (continuing despite difficulty), resilience (the ability to bounce back).
Respectful, people-first language puts the person before the condition: 'a person with a disability', 'an athlete who uses a wheelchair'.
Prefixes make opposites: include/exclude, fair/unfair, able/unable, possible/impossible, accessible/inaccessible.
Adjectives describe nouns (a quick runner); adverbs usually describe verbs (she ran quickly). Many adverbs end in -ly.

example.q: Read: 'When the class planned sports day, Kabir, who uses a wheelchair, expected to sit and watch. But his classmates added a wheelchair relay and a seated ball-throw. That evening Kabir wore a medal and the widest grin on the school bus.' How did the classmates show inclusion?
steps: Notice Kabir's expectation: he thought he would only watch.
Notice what the classmates changed: they added events he could take part in.
The result: he took part and won a medal.
example.answer: They changed the events so that Kabir could take part, instead of leaving him out.

learn.reallife: Ramps beside steps, audio announcements at railway stations and Braille on lift buttons all make places accessible.

games.title: Includes everyone or leaves someone out?
items: Building a ramp beside the stairs
Choosing teams so that everyone gets a turn
Using sign language at assembly
Explaining the rules again for a new student
Laughing at a slow runner
Saying 'You can't play, you're too small'
Planning games only for the fastest players

quiz.q: What does 'inclusion' mean?
options: Making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part
quiz.explain: Inclusion means no one is left out because of ability, background or any difference.
steps: Inclusion = making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part.
Answer: Making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part
quiz.mistake: Confuses inclusion with selection or exclusion

quiz.q: A building is 'accessible' when:
options: it is far from the city
everyone, including people with disabilities, can reach and use it
quiz.explain: Accessible places can be reached and used by everyone, for example with ramps and lifts.
steps: Accessible = easy for everyone, including people with disabilities, to reach and use.
Height or distance has nothing to do with it.
Answer: everyone, including people with disabilities, can reach and use it
quiz.mistake: Thinks accessible just means 'open' or 'near'

quiz.q: What is 'empathy'?
options: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
quiz.explain: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's place and feeling with them.
steps: Empathy = understanding and sharing another person's feelings.
Answer: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
quiz.mistake: Mixes up empathy with a physical quality

quiz.q: Read: 'At the school pool, Nidhi swam a little slower than the others, so her coach gave her a lane of her own and timed her against her own best. By March she had beaten it three times.' What did the coach do?
options: The coach stopped Nidhi from swimming
The coach made Nidhi race against the fastest swimmer
The coach set a fair challenge suited to Nidhi
quiz.explain: Timing Nidhi against her own best is a fair challenge that helped her improve.
steps: The coach gave Nidhi her own lane and timed her against her own best.
That is a fair challenge suited to her, and she improved.
Answer: The coach set a fair challenge suited to Nidhi
quiz.mistake: Picks an action that the passage does not describe

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: 'She ran ___ to the finish line.'
quiz.explain: The word describes how she ran (a verb), so we need the adverb 'quickly'.
steps: The gap describes how she ran, i.e. a verb.
Verbs are described by adverbs; quick + -ly = quickly.
Answer: quickly
quiz.mistake: Uses an adjective to describe a verb

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'include'?
quiz.explain: In- (in) and ex- (out) give the opposites include and exclude.
steps: in- (in) and ex- (out) give opposite meanings.
include ↔ exclude
Answer: Exclude
quiz.mistake: Picks a word that only looks similar

quiz.q: Which is the most respectful way to describe someone?
quiz.explain: People-first language puts the person first and avoids pity or labels.
steps: People-first language puts the person before the condition.
It avoids pity words like helpless, poor thing, weak.
Answer: A person with a disability
quiz.mistake: Uses words of pity that are not respectful

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'perseverance'?
quiz.explain: Perseverance and persistence both mean continuing to try despite difficulties.
steps: Perseverance = continuing despite difficulty.
Persistence means the same.
Answer: Persistence
quiz.mistake: Confuses perseverance with speed or fear

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "My friend has one weak wing. Can he still play our flying games? What does inclusion mean?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Inclusion means everyone gets to take part. We can change the game so my friend flies with us!
teach.nudge: But who should get to play? And what can we change so that nobody is left out?

revise.summary: 'The World of Limitless Possibilities' is linked with sport and inclusion, people of all abilities taking part. The topic builds words like inclusion, accessible, empathy, perseverance and resilience, people-first language, opposite prefixes and adjective vs adverb.
remember: Inclusion = everyone welcomed and able to take part
Accessible = everyone can reach and use it; empathy = sharing another's feelings
traps: Use an adverb to describe a verb: 'ran quickly', not 'ran quick'.
Avoid pity labels like 'that helpless boy'.

learn.hook: Imagine a sports meet where the loudest cheer is not for the fastest runner, but for the bravest try!
points: Special Olympics is a worldwide sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities. It was started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver, and the first International Special Olympics Summer Games were held in Chicago, USA, in 1968.
Its athlete oath is: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.' It values courage and effort over medals alone.
Athletes are grouped with others of similar ability so that every race is fair and everyone has a real chance. In India the movement is run by Special Olympics Bharat.
Unified Sports brings people with and without intellectual disabilities together as teammates.
Sports collocations are words that naturally go together: take part, break a record, win a medal, cross the finish line, cheer on.

example.q: Think it through: What does 'let me be brave in the attempt' mean in the athlete oath?
steps: 'Attempt' means a try or an effort.
The oath first hopes for a win, then says what matters if winning is not possible.
So it asks for courage while trying, whatever the result.
example.answer: It means that even if I don't win, I want to try with courage and give my best effort.

learn.reallife: Many Indian schools hold inclusive sports days and Unified Sports matches where children of all abilities play on the same team.

games.title: Special Olympics facts
items: Special Olympics is a sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities.
That is the group it was created for.
Special Olympics was started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver.
She founded it in the 1960s in the USA.
The first International Special Olympics Summer Games were held in Chicago.
They took place in Chicago, USA, in 1968.
The athlete oath says that only winning matters.
It says that if you cannot win, you should be brave in the attempt.
In Unified Sports, people with and without intellectual disabilities play as teammates.
Unified Sports mixes both groups in one team.

items.text: She ___ the school record in the 100-metre race.
Everyone stood up to ___ on the runners.
Over two hundred students will ___ part in the sports meet.
Priya crossed the finish ___ with a big smile.

quiz.q: Special Olympics is a sports movement mainly for:
quiz.explain: Special Olympics was created to give people with intellectual disabilities the chance to train and compete.
steps: Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities.
Answer: People with intellectual disabilities
quiz.mistake: Confuses Special Olympics with other sports events

quiz.q: The oath says: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.' What does it value most?
quiz.explain: The oath values being brave and trying your best, even without a win.
steps: The oath accepts losing but asks to 'be brave in the attempt'.
So it values courage and effort over medals.
Answer: Courage and effort
quiz.mistake: Stops reading after 'Let me win'

quiz.q: Who started the Special Olympics movement?
quiz.explain: Eunice Kennedy Shriver founded Special Olympics in the 1960s.
steps: Special Olympics was started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver.
Answer: Eunice Kennedy Shriver
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous sports name; Pierre de Coubertin founded the modern Olympic Games, not Special Olympics

quiz.q: What is the Special Olympics programme in India called?
quiz.explain: The programme in India is called Special Olympics Bharat.
steps: In India the movement is run by Special Olympics Bharat.
Answer: Special Olympics Bharat
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with other Indian sports campaigns

quiz.q: What are Unified Sports?
options: Teams where people with and without intellectual disabilities play together
quiz.explain: Unified Sports put athletes with and without intellectual disabilities on the same team.
steps: Unified Sports brings people with and without intellectual disabilities together as teammates.
Answer: Teams where people with and without intellectual disabilities play together
quiz.mistake: Takes 'unified' to mean 'one person'

quiz.q: Read: 'In the 50-metre race, Sana saw Joy trip near the start. She jogged back, helped him up, and they finished together, last but laughing. Their cheer was the loudest of the day.' Why was the cheer loudest for them?
options: The crowd valued their kindness and friendship
quiz.explain: They finished last, so the cheer was for Sana's kindness and their spirit, not their speed.
steps: Sana and Joy finished last, so the cheer was not for speed.
It was for Sana's kindness and their friendship.
Answer: The crowd valued their kindness and friendship
quiz.mistake: Assumes cheers are only for winners

quiz.q: What does 'sportsmanship' mean?
options: Fair and generous behaviour in sport
quiz.explain: Sportsmanship means playing fairly, respecting others and being gracious in winning or losing.
steps: Sportsmanship = fair, generous, respectful behaviour in sport.
Answer: Fair and generous behaviour in sport
quiz.mistake: Thinks the word is about skill or equipment

quiz.q: Which phrase is correct?
quiz.explain: The natural collocation is 'take part in'.
steps: The natural collocation is 'take part in'.
Answer: take part in a race
quiz.mistake: Translates directly from another language without checking the English collocation

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "If a runner doesn't win a medal, did he fail? What is the Special Olympics spirit?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Being brave in the attempt matters more than the medal. Every runner who tries is a winner!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but is winning the only thing that counts? What does the oath ask athletes to be?

revise.summary: Special Olympics, started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver, is a sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities. Its oath values courage over winning, athletes are grouped by ability, and Unified Sports mixes teammates of all abilities.
focus: The athlete oath and its meaning
Unified Sports and Special Olympics Bharat
remember: Founder: Eunice Kennedy Shriver; first International Summer Games: Chicago, 1968
Oath: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.'
Collocations: take part, break a record, win a medal, cross the finish line, cheer on
traps: The oath does not mean winning at any cost.
Say 'take part in', not 'do part' or 'make part'.

topics.title: Nine Gold Medals: a story told in a poem

learn.hook: A poem that tells a whole story, with a twist at the end? That's a narrative poem, and you're about to read one!
points: 'Nine Gold Medals' is a narrative poem about athletes in a race who choose kindness over winning.
A narrative poem tells a story with characters, a setting, events, a climax (the turning point) and an ending.
A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself but holds a deeper truth, for example 'We lost, yet we won'.
Stories in verse usually use the simple past: ran, fell, knelt, cheered.
A good summary gives only the main events in your own words and in the right order, and is much shorter than the original.

example.q:
Read this original narrative poem:
'Our team was one point from the cup
When Meenu's shoelace tangled up;
The rival captain paused the play
And knelt to help her on her way.
We lost the match, the scoreboard said,
But all of us walked home ahead.'
What is the climax, and what is the message?
steps: The tension builds: the team is one point from winning.
The turning point is when the rival captain stops the play to help Meenu.
The last two lines say they lost on the scoreboard but felt like winners.
example.answer: The climax is the rival captain pausing the play to help Meenu. The message: kindness and sportsmanship matter more than the score.

learn.reallife: Think of a time a player in a cricket or football match helped an injured opponent; the crowd often claps more for that than for a goal.

games.title: Story sequence
games.prompt: Put the events of the original poem in order
items: The team needs one more point to win the cup.
Meenu's shoelace gets tangled.
The rival captain pauses the play.
She kneels to help Meenu.
The team loses the match.
Everyone walks home feeling like winners.

items.q: A poem that tells a story
The turning point of a story
A true statement that seems to contradict itself

quiz.q: What is a narrative poem?
options: A poem that tells a story
A poem of only two lines
quiz.explain: A narrative poem tells a story with characters and events.
steps: A narrative poem tells a story with characters and events.
Answer: A poem that tells a story
quiz.mistake: Thinks narrative poems are defined by rhyme or length

quiz.q: 'We lost the match, the scoreboard said, / But all of us walked home ahead.' What is this an example of?
quiz.explain: Losing yet being 'ahead' seems contradictory, but it is true in spirit, so it is a paradox.
steps: 'We lost' yet 'walked home ahead' seems contradictory.
It is true in spirit, so it is a paradox.
Answer: Paradox
quiz.mistake: Looks for 'like' or sound words instead of the idea

quiz.q: 'The rival captain paused the play / And knelt to help her on her way.' What did the rival captain do?
options: She stopped the game to help Meenu
quiz.explain: The lines say she paused the play and knelt to help Meenu.
steps: The lines say she paused the play and knelt to help Meenu.
Answer: She stopped the game to help Meenu
quiz.mistake: Does not read the lines closely

quiz.q: What is the theme of the original poem about Meenu?
options: Kindness matters more than the score
quiz.explain: Even after losing, the team felt they were ahead because of the kindness shown.
steps: The team lost but felt 'ahead' because of the kindness shown.
So the theme is kindness over the score.
Answer: Kindness matters more than the score
quiz.mistake: Focuses on a small detail instead of the main message

quiz.q: What is the climax of a story?
options: The turning point or most intense moment
quiz.explain: The climax is the moment of greatest tension where the story turns.
steps: The climax is the turning point, the most intense moment.
Answer: The turning point or most intense moment
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the climax with the beginning or ending

quiz.q: Which is a good rule for writing a summary?
options: Copy every sentence of the original
Include only the main points in your own words
Add new events of your own
Make it longer than the original
quiz.explain: A summary is short, in your own words, and keeps only the main ideas.
steps: A summary keeps only the main events, in your own words, much shorter.
Answer: Include only the main points in your own words
quiz.mistake: Thinks a summary is a copy or a retelling with extras

quiz.q: What is the simple past of 'kneel'?
quiz.explain: 'Knelt' is the usual past form of 'kneel'.
steps: 'Kneel' is irregular; its usual simple past is 'knelt'.
Answer: knelt
quiz.mistake: Adds -ed or -t without knowing the irregular form

quiz.q: In 'The rival captain paused the play', which word tells us the game stopped only for a short time?
quiz.explain: To pause is to stop for a short time before continuing.
steps: To pause is to stop for a short time before continuing.
Answer: paused
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'paused'

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "How can a team lose a match and still walk home ahead? That makes no sense!"
teach.praise: Chirp! It's a paradox: they lost on the scoreboard but won through kindness. Clever poem!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what did they win, if not the match? What did the captain do?

revise.summary: 'Nine Gold Medals' is a narrative poem about athletes who choose kindness over winning. Readers identify narrative elements, the climax, paradox, simple past verbs, and write short summaries.
remember: Narrative poem = a story in verse: characters, setting, events, climax, ending
Paradox = seems contradictory but holds a deeper truth ('We lost, yet we won')
Simple past in story poems: ran, fell, knelt, cheered
Summary = main events, own words, right order, much shorter
traps: A summary is not a copy of the original and adds no new events.
